summary: At just 1.4 square miles with nearly 7,600 people packed into each of them, Potomac Park is one of the most densely compressed communities in inland Southern California — a census-designated place wedged into the flat, sun-drenched sprawl of the eastern San Joaquin Valley fringe near Bakersfield, where the landscape is agricultural plain in every direction and the sky is enormous. That density, paired with a median home value of roughly $201,000 and a median household income around $45,600, puts the price-to-income ratio near 4.4× — more accessible than coastal California but still a stretch given that nearly 31% of households fall below the poverty line. Rents averaging $1,162 a month consume over 30% of that median income before taxes, which means housing cost burden is a real and measurable pressure here. The climate is emphatically Central Valley: average daytime highs around 81°F, nearly ten hours of sunshine daily, and mild overnight lows near 56°F — summers are genuinely hot, winters brief and mild. With only one school tracked on the CDE dashboard and ELA and math scores well below state benchmarks (–86 and –118 distance from standard, respectively), educational infrastructure is thin on the ground. Employment leans heavily on the agriculture and service sectors that define this part of the valley, making it functionally a commuter node rather than a standalone job center. Potomac Park is a place where the math of California homeownership technically works, but where the income floor and the cost ceiling press uncomfortably close together.
